study_notes.topic: Quantity Comparison (Q1 vs Q2) - Quantitative Aptitude

sections.title: Introduction to Quantity Comparison
sections.content: Quantity Comparison questions do not ask for a single specific numerical answer. Instead, you are given two mathematical statements or problems, labeled Quantity I (Q1) and Quantity II (Q2). Your goal is to evaluate both and determine the relationship between their final values.

sections.title: The Standard Five Options
sections.content: The options are universally standard: A) Q1 > Q2, B) Q1 < Q2, C) Q1 ≥ Q2, D) Q1 ≤ Q2, E) Q1 = Q2 or Relationship Cannot be Established (CND).

sections.title: The 'Do Not Solve Completely' Rule
sections.content: The biggest trap in Q1/Q2 is solving both quantities to the last decimal point. If Q1 clearly evaluates to a number around 50, and Q2 is clearly around 120, you do not need the exact values. Compare the estimated ranges and mark the answer.

sections.title: Basic Algebraic Comparisons
sections.content: Often, Q1 and Q2 involve basic quadratic equations, square roots, or cubes. Apply the same rules as Quadratic Equations: even powers yield two roots (+ and -), while odd powers and square root symbols (√) yield only positive roots.

sections.title: Positive and Negative Value Traps
sections.content: Be highly cautious when variables are involved. If Q1 = x and Q2 = y, and you find x can be -5 or +5 while y is +3, the relationship is CND (because +5 > +3, but -5 < +3).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Wasting time calculating the exact numerical answer when an estimation is sufficient. 2. Forgetting that a square (x²) has both positive and negative roots. 3. Confusing the inequality signs when choosing the final option.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 1 Q1/Q2 questions are essentially two basic math problems combined into one. Focus on speed, use approximation, and stop calculating the moment you can definitively prove one quantity is larger than the other.

short_tricks.topic: Quantity Comparison (Q1 vs Q2) - Quantitative Aptitude

tricks.title: The Approximation Stop
tricks.explanation: If Q1 requires finding 23% of 500, and Q2 requires finding 48% of 600, do not calculate. 23% of 500 is roughly 115. 48% of 600 is nearly half, roughly 300. Q2 is obviously much larger.
tricks.example: Q1 ≈ 115. Q2 ≈ 288. Q1 < Q2. Save 30 seconds by not doing exact multiplication.

tricks.title: The Sign-Only Method
tricks.explanation: If Q1 results in a strictly positive value (e.g., distance, time, or a positive square root) and Q2 results in a strictly negative value, no calculation is needed.
tricks.example: Q1: Time taken by A to finish a job. Q2: The smaller root of x² + 10x + 24 = 0 (Roots are -6, -4). Time is always positive, Q2 is negative. Therefore, Q1 > Q2.

tricks.title: The Root vs Square Trick
tricks.explanation: Understand the difference between Q1: x = √36 and Q2: y² = 36. Q1 is strictly +6. Q2 is +6 and -6.
tricks.example: Comparing +6 to (+6, -6). +6 = +6 and +6 > -6. Therefore, Q1 ≥ Q2.

tricks.title: Direct Elimination of CND
tricks.explanation: If both Q1 and Q2 result in single, fixed numerical values (no variables, no ranges), the answer CANNOT be 'Relationship Cannot be Established'. It must be >, <, or =.
